body.statement: Benchmark normalization gives \(\pi_0(a\mid X)=b_a(X)\) almost surely for every \(a\in\mathcal A\) and makes \(K(\theta)\ge0\) for every \(\theta\in\Theta\). The regular optimizer path is continuously differentiable and satisfies \(H_c\theta_c'=-g_c\), \(\frac{d}{dc}K(\theta_c)=-g_c^\top H_c^{-1}g_c\le0\), and \(\frac{d}{dc}W(\theta_c)=c\frac{d}{dc}K(\theta_c)\). Under feature identification, either \(\theta_c=0\) for every \(c\in\mathcal C\) and the frontier is constant, or \(K(\theta_c)\) is strictly decreasing on \(\mathcal C\); thus a nonconstant maintained frontier has no self-intersection.
body.justification: This result prevents the proposal from manufacturing singular geometry that its own assumptions rule out.
body.gap: FangRidderXie2026 notes that restricted classes need not map preference one-to-one into divergence, but does not state this derivative characterization for the identifiable regular softmax path.
body.consumer: The result tells applied users when ordinary monotone interpolation is safe and when the constant-path set-valued report is necessary.
body.proof_tex:
Write
\[
 Z_x(\theta)=\sum_{r\in\mathcal A}b_r(x)e^{\theta^\top q_r(x)}.
\]
By \(\textnormal{ass:benchmark-normalized}\), \(Z_x(0)=1\).  Hence the formula in
\(\textnormal{def:softmax-rule}\) gives, for every \(a\in\mathcal A\),
\[
 \pi_0(a\mid x)=\frac{b_a(x)}{\sum_{r\in\mathcal A}b_r(x)}=b_a(x)
\]
for almost every \(x\).  For a fixed \(x\) and \(\theta\), put
\(p_a=\pi_\theta(a\mid x)\).  Both \(p_a\) and \(b_a(x)\) are strictly
positive by \(\textnormal{ass:benchmark-positive}\) and the softmax formula,
and both sum to one.  The elementary inequality \(\log u\leq u-1\), applied
with \(u=b_a(x)/p_a\), therefore gives
\[
 \sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p_a\log\frac{p_a}{b_a(x)}
 \geq \sum_{a\in\mathcal A}p_a\left(1-\frac{b_a(x)}{p_a}\right)
 =1-1=0.
\]
Taking \(P_X\)-expectations and using the definition of \(K\) proves
\(K(\theta)\geq0\).  In particular, \(K(0)=0\).

We next establish the regularity of the optimizer path rather than assuming
it.  The integrand defining \(W\) is continuous in \(\theta\) pointwise and
has absolute value at most \(B\), because the declared outcome support
\(Y\in[-B,B]\) implies \(|m_a(X)|\leq B\).  The integrand defining \(K\) is
also pointwise continuous.  Moreover, the preceding nonnegativity argument
and \(b_a(X)\geq\epsilon_b\) yield the uniform bound
\[
 0\leq \sum_a\pi_\theta(a\mid X)
       \log\frac{\pi_\theta(a\mid X)}{b_a(X)}
 \leq \sum_a\pi_\theta(a\mid X)\log\frac1{b_a(X)}
 \leq \log\frac1{\epsilon_b}.
\]
For completeness, pointwise convergence of any one of these bounded
integrands implies convergence of its expectations as follows.  If
\(f_j\to f\) pointwise and \(|f_j|,|f|\leq C\), then for \(\delta>0\) the
sets
\[
 A_N(\delta)=\bigcup_{j\geq N}\{|f_j-f|>\delta\}
\]
decrease to the empty set.  Countable additivity gives
\(P_X(A_N(\delta))\downarrow0\), while for \(j\geq N\),
\[
 E_P|f_j-f|\leq\delta+2C P_X(A_N(\delta)).
\]
First letting \(N\to\infty\) and then \(\delta\downarrow0\) proves the
claim.  Thus \((c,\theta)\mapsto M_c(\theta)=W(\theta)-cK(\theta)\) is
continuous on \(\mathcal C\times\Theta\).

We now prove continuity of \(c\mapsto\theta_c\).  Let \(c_j\to c\).  By
compactness of \(\Theta\), every subsequence of \(\theta_{c_j}\) has a
further subsequence converging to some \(\theta_*\in\Theta\).  For every
\(\vartheta\in\Theta\), optimality in \(\textnormal{def:oracle-path}\)
gives
\[
 M_{c_j}(\theta_{c_j})\geq M_{c_j}(\vartheta).
\]
Passing to the convergent subsequence and using the continuity just proved
gives \(M_c(\theta_*)\geq M_c(\vartheta)\).  Assumption
\(\textnormal{ass:unique-optimizer}\) forces \(\theta_*=\theta_c\).  Since
every convergent subsequence has this same limit, \(\theta_{c_j}\to\theta_c\).

Fix \(c_0\in\mathcal C\), write \(\theta_0=\theta_{c_0}\), and define
\[
 F(c,\theta)=\nabla_\theta M_c(\theta).
\]
Assumption \(\textnormal{ass:uniform-interior}\) makes \(\theta_0\) an
interior maximizer, so \(F(c_0,\theta_0)=0\).  We record why the derivatives
of \(W\) and \(K\) used below follow from the stated smoothness condition.
Choose \(c_1\in\mathcal C\), \(c_1\neq c_0\), sufficiently close to
\(c_0\).  On a common neighborhood of \(\theta_0\),
\[
 K(\theta)=\frac{M_{c_0}(\theta)-M_{c_1}(\theta)}{c_1-c_0},
 \qquad
 W(\theta)=M_{c_0}(\theta)+c_0K(\theta).
\]
Thus \(\textnormal{ass:smooth-criterion}\) makes \(W\) and \(K\) three
times continuously differentiable there.  Consequently \(F\) is
continuously differentiable in \((c,\theta)\), and
\[
 \partial_\theta F(c_0,\theta_0)
 =\nabla_\theta^2M_{c_0}(\theta_0)=-H_{c_0}.
\]
This matrix is invertible by \(\textnormal{ass:uniform-curvature}\).

Here is a direct local continuation argument.  Set
\(A_0=\partial_\theta F(c_0,\theta_0)\) and
\(T_c(\theta)=\theta-A_0^{-1}F(c,\theta)\).  Continuity of
\(\partial_\theta F\) permits a closed ball \(D\) about \(\theta_0\) and
an interval \(I\) about \(c_0\), relative to \(\mathcal C\), such that
\[
 \sup_{(c,\theta)\in I\times D}
 \left\|I_d-A_0^{-1}\partial_\theta F(c,\theta)\right\|\leq\frac12
\]
and \(\|T_c(\theta_0)-\theta_0\|\) is at most half the radius of \(D\).
The mean-value integral then shows that \(T_c\) maps \(D\) into itself and
contracts distances by at most \(1/2\).  Starting from \(\theta_0\), its
iterates have successive distances bounded by a geometric series, hence
converge in the closed Euclidean ball \(D\) to a fixed point; the same
contraction inequality makes that fixed point unique.  Denote it by
\(\eta(c)\).  The contraction inequality also gives continuity of
\(\eta\) in \(c\).  The already proved continuity of \(\theta_c\) places
\(\theta_c\) in \(D\) for all \(c\) close enough to \(c_0\); interiority
gives \(F(c,\theta_c)=0\), and uniqueness of the fixed point therefore gives
\(\eta(c)=\theta_c\).

For a small increment \(t\), the identity
\(F(c+t,\theta_{c+t})=F(c,\theta_c)=0\), the exact linearity of \(F\) in
\(c\), and the mean-value integral in \(\theta\) give
\[
 0=A_t(\theta_{c+t}-\theta_c)-t\nabla K(\theta_c),
 \qquad
 A_t=\int_0^1\partial_\theta F\bigl(c+t,
       \theta_c+s(\theta_{c+t}-\theta_c)\bigr)\,ds.
\]
As \(t\to0\), \(A_t\to-H_c\); these matrices are invertible for all small
\(t\).  Hence
\[
 \theta_c'=(-H_c)^{-1}g_c=-H_c^{-1}g_c,
 \qquad\text{or equivalently}\qquad H_c\theta_c'=-g_c.
\]
The displayed derivative is continuous in \(c\).  Since \(c_0\) was
arbitrary, the local paths glue to a continuously differentiable path on
\(\mathcal C\), with the usual one-sided interpretation at its endpoints.

The interior first-order condition also states
\[
 0=\nabla M_c(\theta_c)=a_c-cg_c,
 \qquad\text{so}\qquad a_c=cg_c.
\]
The chain rule and the preceding path equation now yield, equation by
equation,
\[
 \frac{d}{dc}K(\theta_c)
 =g_c^\top\theta_c'
 =-g_c^\top H_c^{-1}g_c\leq0
\]
and
\[
 \frac{d}{dc}W(\theta_c)
 =a_c^\top\theta_c'
 =c g_c^\top\theta_c'
 =c\frac{d}{dc}K(\theta_c).
\]
The inequality follows because \(H_c\) is positive definite under
\(\textnormal{ass:uniform-curvature}\).

It remains to prove the claimed strict dichotomy.  We first show that
\(g_c\neq0\) whenever \(\theta_c\neq0\).  Fix such a \(c\) and abbreviate
\(\theta=\theta_c\).  For each \(x\), let
\[
 \ell_x(t)=\log\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}b_a(x)e^{t\theta^\top q_a(x)},
 \qquad
 k_x(t)=\sum_a\pi_{t\theta}(a\mid x)
            \log\frac{\pi_{t\theta}(a\mid x)}{b_a(x)}.
\]
Finite summation and direct differentiation give
\[
 k_x(t)=t\ell_x'(t)-\ell_x(t),
 \qquad
 k_x'(t)=t\ell_x''(t)
 =t\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_{t\theta}}
       (\theta^\top q_A(x)\mid X=x).
\]
Uniform interiority ensures that \((1+s)\theta\in\Theta\) for all
sufficiently small \(s>0\).  Hence
\[
 r_s(x)=\frac{k_x(1+s)-k_x(1)}s\geq0,
 \qquad
 r_s(x)\longrightarrow
 V(x):=\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_\theta}
       (\theta^\top q_A(x)\mid X=x).
\]
By \(\textnormal{ass:feature-identification}\), \(P_X\{V>0\}>0\).
Thus there are \(\delta>0\) and a measurable set \(E\) with
\(P_X(E)>0\) such that \(V\geq2\delta\) on \(E\).  To avoid hiding any
limit interchange, take an arbitrary sequence \(s_j\downarrow0\) and set
\[
 E_N=E\cap\bigcap_{j\geq N}\{r_{s_j}\geq\delta\}.
\]
Pointwise convergence gives \(E_N\uparrow E\), so
\(P_X(E_N)\uparrow P_X(E)\).  For every \(j\geq N\),
\[
 E_P r_{s_j}\geq\delta P_X(E_N).
\]
On the other hand, differentiability of \(K\), established above, implies
\[
 \theta^\top g_c
 =\lim_{s\downarrow0}\frac{K((1+s)\theta)-K(\theta)}s
 =\lim_{s\downarrow0}E_P r_s
 \geq\delta P_X(E)>0.
\]
Because the sequence was arbitrary, the last inequality holds for the full
right-hand limit.  Therefore \(g_c\neq0\) whenever \(\theta_c\neq0\).

Finally, suppose \(\theta_{c_0}=0\) for some \(c_0\).  Since \(K\geq0\),
\(K(0)=0\), and zero is interior by
\(\textnormal{ass:uniform-interior}\), differentiability gives
\(\nabla K(0)=0\).  Local continuous differentiability of \(K\) makes its
gradient locally Lipschitz: \(\|\nabla K(u)-\nabla K(0)\|\leq L\|u\|\).
The path equation and \(\|H_c^{-1}\|\leq h^{-1}\) consequently imply, on
a sufficiently small interval about \(c_0\),
\[
 \|\theta_c\|
 \leq \frac{L}{h}\left|\int_{c_0}^{c}\|\theta_s\|\,ds\right|.
\]
For \(c\geq c_0\), if
\(U(c)=\int_{c_0}^c\|\theta_s\|\,ds\), then
\(U'(c)\leq(L/h)U(c)\) and \(U(c_0)=0\); differentiating
\(e^{-Lc/h}U(c)\) shows \(U=0\).  The same argument with reversed limits
handles \(c\leq c_0\).  Thus the zero set
\(\{c\in\mathcal C:\theta_c=0\}\) is open; it is closed by continuity of
the path.  Since \(\mathcal C\) is an interval, this set is either empty or
all of \(\mathcal C\).

If it is all of \(\mathcal C\), then
\((W(\theta_c),K(\theta_c))=(W(0),0)\) for every \(c\), so the frontier is
constant.  Otherwise \(\theta_c\neq0\) for every \(c\), whence
\(g_c\neq0\) and
\[
 \frac{d}{dc}K(\theta_c)=-g_c^\top H_c^{-1}g_c<0.
\]
The mean-value theorem makes \(K(\theta_c)\) strictly decreasing on
\(\mathcal C\).  Its value is therefore an injective coordinate of the
frontier, so two distinct penalty values cannot produce the same
\((W,K)\) pair.  This proves the no-self-intersection conclusion for every
nonconstant maintained frontier.
